usage: I top up the transit card.
The transit card balance is low.
Can I use a transit card?
asking in a cab or shop
examples: I topped up my transit card at the convenience store.
교통카드만 있으면 버스랑 지하철 다 탈 수 있어요.
If you just have a transit card, you can take both the bus and subway.
These days people use a transit card on their phone too.
nuance: 교통카드 is the rechargeable card (T머니, 캐시비, or a 후불 credit card) you tap to ride buses, the subway, and even pay some taxis; the verb is 찍다 (to tap), not 누르다. You 충전 (top up) a prepaid one at convenience stores or subway machines, and the gate beeps your 잔액 (remaining balance) so you know when to reload.
mistakes: Don't confuse 교통카드 with a regular 카드 (credit/debit card); the transit card is the tap-to-ride one.
Use 교통카드를 찍다 (tap), not 교통카드를 누르다.

examples: Since I take the subway every day, I bought a commuter pass.
The commuter pass lets you ride 60 times over 30 days.
You can't take the bus with a (subway) commuter pass.
nuance: 정기권 is a period/commuter pass that's cheaper than paying per ride if you commute daily; Seoul's subway 정기권 is a 30-day, 60-trip card loaded onto a special card. Note the standard subway 정기권 only works on the subway (not buses, and no free 환승 to buses), so do the math before buying one. The verb for getting one is 끊다 or 충전하다.
mistakes: Don't assume the subway 정기권 includes bus transfers; it usually doesn't.
Don't confuse 정기권 (period pass) with a single-ride 일회용 ticket.

usage: I have to catch the last train.
The last train is gone (service ended).
examples: Let's hurry before the last train is gone.
The subway's last train is usually around midnight.
I missed the last train, so I came by taxi.
nuance: 막차 (literally 'last vehicle') is a huge deal in Korean nightlife since the subway stops around midnight and missing it means an expensive taxi. You'll constantly hear 막차 끊기다 (service ends) and 막차 놓치다 (miss it); checking the 막차 시간 before drinking is a real survival habit. Its opposite is 첫차.
mistakes: Don't say 막차를 잃어버렸어요 (lost it); to miss a train is 막차를 놓치다.
막차 시간 is the departure time of the last train, not the arrival time, so leave early enough to actually board it.

english: first train / first bus of the day
usage: What time is the first train?
I go on the first train.
examples: I took the first train to go to the airport.
The subway's first train usually runs around 5:30.
I stayed up all night and went home on the first train.
nuance: 첫차 (literally 'first vehicle') is the earliest departure of the day, the counterpart to 막차; the subway 첫차 usually runs around 5:30 a.m. People take the 첫차 for early flights or after staying out all night (밤새우다). The verb 다니다 (to run/operate) is common for describing when it runs.
mistakes: Don't write 첫 차 with a space; the word for first train is 첫차 (one word).
Don't confuse 첫차 (first departure) with 첫째 (the first one in order).

examples: It snowed a lot, so the train was delayed 30 minutes.
I was late to my appointment because of the delay.
The KTX was delayed, so I got a refund.
nuance: 연착 is a delay in arrival or departure for trains, buses, or flights; you'll hear it in station announcements as 연착 안내. The usual verb forms are 연착되다 and 연착하다, and for long KTX/SRT delays you can sometimes get partial compensation (보상). It contrasts with arriving 정시에 (on time).
mistakes: Don't use 늦다 alone for a vehicle running late; the proper transit word is 연착되다.
Don't confuse 연착 (a transport delay) with 지각 (a person being late, e.g. to work).

usage: The express doesn't stop at this station.
examples: If you take the express, you get there 20 minutes faster.
이 역에는 급행이 안 서니까 일반을 타세요.
The express doesn't stop at this station, so take the local.
The Line 9 express is always crowded.
nuance: 급행 is express service (on lines like Seoul Subway Line 9 or the GTX) that skips smaller stations to save time; its opposite is 완행 or 일반 (local/all-stops). Crucially, the 급행 doesn't stop everywhere, so check whether it stops (서다) at your destination before boarding. People weigh the time saved against often heavier crowding.
mistakes: Don't board a 급행 without checking if it stops at your station; it skips many.
Don't confuse 급행 (express service) with 급하다 (to be in a hurry).

usage: I get off at the next stop.
Please exit through the back door.
examples: 내릴 때 카드를 안 찍으면 하차 처리가 안 돼요.
If you don't tap your card when getting off, the tag-off isn't registered.
When getting off the bus, please use the rear door.
하차 벨을 미리 눌러야 기사님이 세워 줘요.
You have to press the bell in advance so the driver stops.
nuance: 하차 is the formal word for getting off a bus or train, the counterpart to 승차; in daily speech people just say 내리다. It matters most on buses, where you must do a 하차 태그 (tap your card when getting off) to get the free transfer (환승), and you press the 하차 벨 to signal your stop. Exit through the 뒷문 (rear door) is the norm.
mistakes: Don't forget the 하차 태그 on buses; skipping it can void your transfer discount.
Don't confuse 하차 (getting off) with 승차 (getting on).

usage: I board through the front door.
examples: You board the bus through the front and get off through the back.
It's convenient to buy your ticket in advance.
밤에 택시 승차 거부를 당한 적이 있어요.
I've been refused a ride by a taxi at night.
nuance: 승차 is the formal term for boarding/getting on, paired with 하차; casually people say 타다. You'll see it in 승차권 (a fare ticket) and the well-known phrase 승차 거부 (a taxi illegally refusing a passenger), a real frustration late at night. On buses the rule is 앞문 승차, 뒷문 하차.
mistakes: Don't confuse 승차 (boarding) with 하차 (getting off).
Don't say 승차권 for a transit card; 승차권 is a single ticket, the card is a 교통카드.

usage: I go through the fare gate.
I tap my card at the gate.
Let's meet in front of the gate.
examples: The gate wouldn't open because my balance was too low.
Once you pass the fare gate, the platform is right there.
I'll wait in front of the fare gate.
nuance: 개찰구 is the subway/train fare gate where you tap your 교통카드 to enter and exit; if your 잔액 is too low it won't open and beeps at you. It's also one of the most common places Koreans say they'll meet ('개찰구 앞에서 봐'). The platform itself is the 승강장.
mistakes: Don't confuse 개찰구 (the fare gate) with 출입구 (a building entrance/exit).
Remember to tap at the 개찰구 both entering and exiting, or you may be overcharged.

usage: I look at the route map.
examples: 처음 왔을 때 지하철 노선도가 너무 복잡했어요.
When I first arrived, the subway route map was so complicated.
이 버스 노선이 우리 집 앞을 지나가요.
This bus route passes in front of my house.
앱에서 노선이랑 시간표를 확인할 수 있어요.
You can check the route and timetable in the app.
nuance: 노선 means a transit route or line, used for both buses and subway lines; the famous 노선도 (route map) is the colored subway map newcomers stare at. For subways, casual speech uses 호선 (e.g. 2호선 = Line 2), while 노선 is the more general word for a route's path. Apps like 카카오맵 or 네이버지도 show every 노선 and timetable.
mistakes: Don't confuse 노선 (the route/line) with 노선도 (the map of routes).
For a specific subway line, Koreans usually say the number + 호선, not just 노선.

usage: I change lines at the transfer station.
The next stop is a transfer station.
I get off at the transfer station.
examples: Sadang is a transfer station for Lines 2 and 4.
Transfer to Line 5 at the transfer station.
환승역은 걷는 거리가 길어서 시간이 좀 걸려요.
Transfer stations have long walking distances, so it takes some time.
nuance: 환승역 is a station where two or more subway lines meet so you can 갈아타다 (transfer); big ones like 사당, 신도림, or 왕십리 are notoriously crowded and involve long underground walks. Free transfers between subway and bus depend on tapping your 교통카드 within the time limit, not just on being at a 환승역.
mistakes: Don't confuse 환승역 (a transfer station) with 종점 (the last stop/terminal).
Don't assume any station lets you transfer; only a 환승역 connects multiple lines.

english: terminal, last stop (end of the line)
usage: I get off at the last stop.
I go all the way to the terminal.
examples: I dozed off and ended up riding to the last stop.
Where is this bus's last stop?
The bus heads to the depot from the last stop, so everyone get off.
nuance: 종점 is the final stop where a bus or subway route ends, the opposite of 첫 정거장 (the first stop); the driver will announce 'here is the 종점, everyone off.' Falling asleep and riding to the 종점 (종점까지 가다) is a relatable mishap. For express buses between cities the bigger hub is a 터미널, while 종점 is the end of a local route.
mistakes: Don't confuse 종점 (the end of a route) with 환승역 (a mid-route transfer station).
Don't use 종점 for an intercity bus terminal; that larger hub is a 터미널.
